t.1.61.1: O best of men, O delight of the Raghus, the greatly renowned king, having taken Śunaḥśepa, rested at midday at Puṣkara.
t.1.61.2: While he was resting there, the illustrious Śunaḥśepa came to the excellent Puṣkara and saw Viśvāmitra.
t.1.61.3: Downcast of face and wretched from thirst and weariness, he fell into the lap of the sage, O Rāma, and spoke these words.
t.1.61.4: I have no mother, no father; how then could I have kinsmen or relatives? O gentle one, O bull among sages, you ought to protect me in accordance with dharma.
t.1.61.6: Having performed unsurpassed austerity, may I attain the world of heaven. Be my protector, for I am without a protector, with a gracious mind; O righteous-souled one, you ought to save me from sin as a father saves his son.
t.1.61.5: You indeed are the protector, O best of sages; you indeed are the sustainer of all. Let the king accomplish his purpose, and let me be long-lived and unharmed.
t.1.61.7: Having heard those words of his, Viśvāmitra of great austerity comforted him in many ways and then spoke these words to his sons.
t.1.61.8: That for the sake of which fathers, seeking what is good, beget sons, for the welfare of the world beyond, the time for that has now arrived.
t.1.61.9: This young boy, the son of a sage, seeks refuge from me. My dear sons, do what is pleasing to me by granting him nothing less than his life.
t.1.61.11: Then Śunaḥśepa would have a protector, the sacrifice would proceed without hindrance, the deities would be satisfied, and my word too would be fulfilled.
t.1.61.10: All of you who have done good deeds, all of you devoted to dharma, become the king's sacrificial victims and give satisfaction to Agni.
t.1.61.12: Having heard the words of the sage, O best of men, his sons, Madhuṣyanda and the others, spoke this with arrogance and in mockery.
t.1.61.13: How can you, O lord, abandon your own sons and save the son of another? We regard this as something not to be done, like dog's flesh in a meal.
t.1.61.14: Having heard those words of his sons, the bull among sages, his eyes reddened with anger, began to speak.
t.1.61.15: This has been spoken without fear, a thing condemned even by dharma, in overstepping my word, stern and hair-raising as it is.
t.1.61.17: Then the best of sages, having made his sons subject to a curse, and having provided a flawless protection, spoke to the distressed Śunaḥśepa.
t.1.61.16: Like the sons of Vasiṣṭha, all of you shall be born among the low castes as eaters of dog's flesh, and you shall dwell upon the earth for a full thousand years.
t.1.61.18: Bound with the sacred cords and adorned with red garlands and unguents, when you have come to the sacrificial post of Viṣṇu, invoke Agni with words of praise.
t.1.61.20: Śunaḥśepa, having received those two verses and with his mind well composed, hastily spoke to Ambarīṣa, that lion among kings.
t.1.61.19: But you, O son of a sage, should sing these two divine verses at this sacrifice of Ambarīṣa; then you will attain success.
t.1.61.21: O lion among kings, O mighty one, let us two go quickly to the sacrificial assembly; turn back, O lord of kings, and undertake the consecration.
t.1.61.22: Having heard those words of the sage's son, the king, joyful and eager, went swiftly and untiringly to the sacrificial enclosure.
t.1.61.24: Bound, the young son of the sage duly praised the two gods, Indra and Indra's younger brother, with the finest words.
t.1.61.25: Then the thousand-eyed one, pleased and gratified by the secret hymns of praise, granted long life to Śunaḥśepa, O Rāghava.
t.1.61.26: And that king, O best of men, O Rāma, obtained the manifold fruit of the sacrifice, born of the grace of the thousand-eyed Indra.
t.1.61.27: And Viśvāmitra too, the righteous-souled one of great austerity, once again performed penance at Puṣkara, O best of men, for a thousand years.
t.1.61.23: With the consent of the members of the sacrificial assembly, the king had the victim marked with the purifying sacred grass and clothed in red garments, and then bound him to the sacrificial post.
